respite

/RES-pit/ - the stress falls on RES · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Respite means a short period of rest or relief from something difficult.

The ceasefire gave the border villages a two-week respite, long enough to bring in the harvest.

Worked Example

When the monsoon finally paused, the road crews got a five-day respite: time to patch the washouts, shore up the hillside, and sleep past dawn for the first time in a month. Nobody mistook it for the end of the rains — the second front was already on the forecast.

Respite is more exact than break because it requires hardship on both sides of it: a coffee break interrupts an ordinary morning, but a respite is carved out of something genuinely punishing, and everyone knows the punishment resumes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

reprieve: A reprieve is relief that someone with power grants — the execution stayed, the deadline pushed back, the closure postponed. It comes down from a decision. A respite needs no one's signature: the shelling pauses, the fever breaks, the pain lets up. Both are temporary; only a reprieve is issued.

lull: A lull is a quiet spell in the activity itself — the wind drops, the shelling thins, the orders stop coming in. It is measured from outside and need not be felt as relief by anyone. A respite is defined by the sufferer: relief from hardship, felt as relief, with the hardship waiting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

onslaught: a sustained attack or flood of demands

grind: unrelenting, wearing work

Where it sits · how lasting the relief is — breather → respite → deliverance

breather vs. respite: A breather is seconds or minutes snatched mid-effort; respite goes further — a real stretch of relief in which the pressure genuinely lifts.

deliverance vs. respite: Deliverance goes far beyond respite: a respite ends and the hardship returns, while deliverance means being rescued from it once and for all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back

Root — spite

Root — spite: a look (Latin specere, spectus, to look)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (back) + spite (a look) = a looking back. In medieval French law, a respit was time granted to look at a matter again before judgment — a delay. From 'time to look again' the word softened into today's sense: a stretch of relief carved out of hardship.

Use the root in a new word: respect

Use the root in a new word: respect: The rookie earned the crew's respect one careful weld at a time.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Respite needs hardship to push against: heat, grief, shelling, double shifts. For a pause with nothing painful around it, break or lull is the honest word. Its cluster-mate repose is the resting itself — during a respite from the grind, you might finally repose.
